name: The Choukouzan Weeping Cherry
access: Free, on a public walking course through the former Shotaiji temple grounds (the temple's main halls were lost to fire in the 1850s and again in 1915); no gate or entry fee.
transport: Iriuda Station (Hakone Tozan Line), about 20 minutes uphill on foot.
verify_notes: Also known as Chokozan no Shidarezakura (long-form: Choukouzan Shoutaiji no Shidarezakura). Stands on the former grounds of Shotaiji temple, the Odawara Inaba clan's family temple; the temple's main halls burned in the Ansei era (1850s) and its last surviving gate burned in 1915, so only this cherry, 360 stone steps and eight Inaba-clan graves remain on site, now part of a signposted historic-site walking course. Designated an Odawara City Natural Monument on 1957-03-30 and one of the 'Kanagawa Meiboku 100' famous trees in 1984 (Kanagawa Arborists Association). A 2007 tree survey (cited by Japanese Wikipedia, sourced to a Kanagawa Arborists Association PDF) recorded height 12.7m, breast-height girth 4.66m, base girth 8.0m, crown spread roughly 7-10.3m in each direction. Age: the same 2007 source calls it 'an estimated 300 years or more'; separately, Japanese Wikipedia states the tree is presumed (hedged, 'presumed'/suitei) to have been planted as a garden tree around 1669 when the temple relocated to Iryuda, which would put it at roughly 357 years old in 2026. Both figures converge on 'several centuries, call it roughly 350 years' rather than agreeing on a precise number; other secondary sources round to '340 years' or '360 years'. Famous flower-viewing spot, late March to early April; queues reportedly form from Iriuda Station at peak bloom, and it is listed as a current hanami destination on jorudan.co.jp's 2026 flower-viewing feature page, which is the best 'alive now' evidence found. Vigor concerns in the late 1980s/1990s led Sumitomo Forestry to begin cloning the tree in 2003, succeeding by 2009; the clones now grow at the temple and at a nearby children's park, which is evidence the tree's decline was being actively managed rather than that the tree was lost. Species read as Prunus itosakura, weeping form (shidarezakura); ask the reader to confirm the exact cultivar. Container judgement: nearest published Ancient Trees city is Kamakura, roughly 40km / 45+ minutes away by train, outside day-trip range, so this ships as its own single-tree place, Odawara, under the 2026-08-31 exception (a well-documented, officially designated, actively publicized flower-viewing destination people specifically travel to see in bloom season).

name: The Eimeiji Osmanthus

location.address: Nakano 2933, Ora, Ora District, Gunma Prefecture, Japan

access: Free; on the grounds of Eimeiji, a Soto Zen temple that Ora town's own education board actively documents as a public flower-viewing spot every September-October, open in daylight hours.
transport: Honnakano Station, about 10 minutes on foot (1km); Shinozuka Station is a further alternative, about 22 minutes on foot (1.7km).
verify_notes: A nationally designated Natural Monument (kuni shitei tennen kinenbutsu) since Showa 12, 1937, which is a notably high designation tier for an osmanthus rather than a more typical giant conifer or camphor. Ora town's own education-board page (updated 2022, with a full season of dated bloom photographs from late September through early October, including a rare second bloom) is the strongest 'alive now' evidence found: it shows the tree flowering in real time within the last few years. The tree was originally a 16m giant; a typhoon in Showa 41 (1966) felled it, and shoots that regrew from the trunk/stump have since grown back. The two sources disagree on how tall the regrowth now stands (town page: 7m; nihon-kankou.or.jp, the national tourism federation: 5m), which is plausible as different survey years rather than a real conflict, and is recorded rather than resolved. Girth given here (330cm / 3.3m) and crown spread (18m east-west, 14m north-south) are from nihon-kankou.or.jp and describe the ORIGINAL pre-1966 trunk; no updated girth for the regrown stems was found in either source, so treat 330cm as historical rather than current, and flag this for a reader with a tape measure. Age conflicts between the two sources and is delivered as both figures rather than picked: the town page states 'age 750 years' (undated basis); nihon-kankou.or.jp states the tree dates from Genko 1 (1331), which is roughly 695 years as of 2026. Both point to 'several centuries, likely 700+ years' rather than a precise number. Location: OSM places Eimeiji itself at 36.2620412,139.4628099 (matches the lead's given coordinates closely), but that is the temple's footprint, not a tree-level pin verified independently of the building, so location_precision is approximate rather than confirmed. Container judgement: no published Ancient Trees city sits within day-trip range of Ora, Gunma (Tokyo is roughly 70km/well over an hour away). Ships as its own single-tree place, Ora, under the 2026-08-31 exception: a nationally protected specimen with its own dedicated, actively updated town tourism page and a real seasonal following (kinmokusei-viewing is a genuine autumn tradition in Japan, distinct from but comparable to hanami).

name: The Wisteria of Fujishima
age_estimate: several hundred years, one account says over 400

location.address: Kozuya Nishoji, Ichinohe, Ninohe District, Iwate Prefecture, Japan

access: Free, on an open, signposted natural-monument site next to Kozuya Elementary School; a Benzaiten shrine stands at its base and it hosts an annual Wisteria Festival on the last Sunday of May with night illumination.
transport: Kozuya Station (IGR Iwate Ginga Railway), about 10 minutes on foot; about 15 minutes by car from Ichinohe Interchange on the Hachinohe Expressway.
verify_notes: One of only 8 vine-form trees ever given Japan's national Natural Monument designation (7 wisteria plus one Bauhinia championii), and the northernmost of them; designated 1938-12-14 (Showa 13). The name Fujishima ('wisteria island') comes from a moat that once ran on three sides of the site, making it look like an island. At designation it was reportedly Japan's largest wisteria, but typhoon damage and trunk rot have cost it some of its vine mass since; a 1954 typhoon (Toya-maru) felled its main stem, and it has grown on a steel trellis/scaffold ever since. A 2022 Asahi Shimbun article (used as one of the two independent sources here, alongside Japanese Wikipedia's citation trail to published print references) reports the tree in good bloom that May and covers an ongoing conservation programme run partly by schoolchildren from the adjacent Kozuya Elementary School, which is solid recent alive-and-tended evidence. Age is given only vaguely by the sources ('several hundred years, one account says over 400') and is repeated here as vaguely as given rather than sharpened. Girth: a 1969 survey recorded root circumference (ne-mawari, not necessarily a standard breast-height girth given the tree is a climbing vine on a support structure) of 3.6m; other secondary sources round this to 3.3m or 4m, so treat 360cm as the best-sourced figure with real spread around it. Height is hard to state for a vine trained up a trellis; sources describe supported growth reaching over 20m. The trunk/main stems are internally rotted and split into seven pieces per the 1995 reference book Wikipedia cites, but the bark-adjacent wood is described as healthy and overall vigour as good. An adjacent, town-designated pair of wisteria stumps ('Kannondo no Fuji') grew from this tree's own seed, which is corroborating evidence of a long-established, well-studied specimen rather than an isolated claim. Container judgement: no published Ancient Trees city is within day-trip range of Ichinohe, Iwate (a rural town in northern Iwate, well outside any of Tokyo/Kyoto/Osaka/Nara/Sapporo's reach). Ships as its own single-tree place, Ichinohe, under the 2026-08-31 exception: a rare national-tier vine-tree designation with an annual festival and night illumination that people specifically travel for during the bloom window.

name: The Great Muku of Futami
access: ACCESS UNCERTAIN, see verify_notes: Gojo City's own page states the tree stands in a private residence's garden ('minka no niwa'), but that its crown spreads out over the adjoining municipal road, so it is visible from and stands partly over public ground even though the trunk itself is not enterable.
transport: Yamato-Futami Station (JR Wakayama Line), about 6 to 10 minutes on foot.
verify_notes: ACCESS JUDGEMENT HELD PENDING A DECISION, not silently shipped and not silently dropped: Gojo City's own tourism page (updated 2022-12-16, the most current source found and the best 'alive now' evidence) says plainly the tree stands 'in the garden of a private residence' (minka no niwa ni arimasu) at Futami 4-chome, but that its branches and foliage spread out substantially over the municipal road (shido ni kakete ooki-ku edaha wo shigerasete imasu). So the trunk sits on private land, not genuinely open to enter, while the canopy is genuinely visible and reachable to stand under from the public street. This is the same shape as the project's established 'view-only tree' pattern (a tree visible from public ground even though its base is not reachable) but it is close enough to the private-land line that it is recorded here rather than assumed either way; a later pass or Hidde should make the final access call, and the pin above marks the tree itself, not a separated viewing point, so it should be re-checked before anything ships. Nationally designated Natural Monument since 1957-05-08 (Showa 32) and separately selected for the 'New Japan 100 Famous Trees' list (Shin Nihon Meiboku Hyakusen), which is strong evidence this specific tree, not just its species, draws visitors deliberately; that selection is what clears the single-tree-destination bar for its container judgement below. Breast-height girth 8.5m (850cm) and current height about 15m are consistent across the Gojo City page and the Nara Prefectural Library page. The tree's main trunk broke in the 1959 Ise Bay Typhoon (Typhoon Vera); pre-storm height is given inconsistently across secondary sources as 25m or 30m, neither of which is the official city figure, so only the current post-storm 15m is used here and the taller figures are noted rather than used. Age is given only as 'over 1,000 years' or 'approximately 1,000 years' across multiple secondary sources with no cited derivation (no growth-rate or documented-planting basis found), so it is repeated here as vaguely as the sources give it, with a deliberately wide band. Container judgement: no published Ancient Trees city sits within day-trip range (Nara city is roughly 40km / well over an hour away by train). Ships as its own single-tree place, Gojo, under the 2026-08-31 exception, on the strength of the national-monument designation plus the New Japan 100 Famous Trees selection.
